title: Twin tremors rock Nagpur rural, 15th quake since 2023, revive seismic concern
text: AI image Nagpur: Two mild earthquakes struck villages in Nagpur district on Tuesday, making it the 15th recorded seismic activity in the cityâs hinterland since 2023 and renewing concerns among geologists over a steady rise in earthquake activity in an area traditionally considered among the safest seismic zones in the country. However, there was no loss of life or property. According to National Centre for Seismology (NCS), a 2.3-magnitude earthquake was recorded at Haldgaon village in Umred tehsil around 3.30pm, followed by a 3.0-magnitude tremor near neighbouring Dawaha village, 26km off Nagpur city. The twin tremors, which originated 8-10km beneath the earthâs surface, added to the growing list of earthquakes reported from the Nagpur region, which recorded two seismic events in 2023 and 11 in 2024 alone. The temblors come against the backdrop of a series of significant seismic events experienced across Vidarbha in the last two years. In December 2024, a 5.3-magnitude earthquake in Mulugu, Telangana, sent strong tremors across Nagpur and several districts of Vidarbha, an event widely considered the strongest in the region since the devastating 1997 Latur earthquake. Earlier, Melghat in Amravati district was jolted by a 4.2-magnitude earthquake, while Seoni in neighbouring Madhya Pradesh also witnessed tremors that sent ripples in the region. Though Umred hosts several open-cast mines operated by Western Coalfields (WCL), where blasting often causes vibrations in nearby villages, experts said Wednesdayâs events were different because they were recorded well below the surface and bore characteristics of natural earthquakes rather than mining-induced disturbances. The twin tremors occurred on a day when Korba in Chhattisgarh also reported a 3.5-magnitude earthquake. Earlier this month, Ghugus in Chandrapur district recorded a 2.7-magnitude tremor. Maharashtra has witnessed a cluster of low-intensity earthquakes in recent weeks, including two events in Palghar measuring 2.1 and 2.4 magnitude, a 2.6-magnitude earthquake near Pune and a 3.3-magnitude tremor in Sangli. Former director of Earthquake Geology Division, GSI, Anjan Chatterjee said the increasing frequency of earthquakes around Nagpur cannot be dismissed as isolated. âThese locations are 20km southeast of Nagpur. But the aggravation of seismic activities in and around Nagpur in the past five years is a matter of concern. Never have so many tremors been recorded in or around Nagpur, thus busting the myth that we are in the safest seismic zone, namely Zone II under BIS classification,â he said. Chatterjee said detailed investigations, including deep seismic sounding studies, are required to understand the processes triggering the earthquakes. He believes the tremors may indicate recent reactivation of dormant faults at depths of around 8km, matching the focal depth of Tuesdayâs events. The rise in seismic activity had earlier prompted Geological Survey of India (GSI) to undertake a comprehensive study after a series of low-intensity earthquakes struck Nagpur district in May 2024. The study covered 21 villages across Parseoni, Kuhi, Umred and Kamptee tehsils, followed by a micro-earthquake survey spread over nearly 1,400 sqkm. GSI also recommended heightened monitoring and adherence to earthquake-resistant construction norms. While Nagpur continues to fall under Seismic Zone II, experts say the growing number of tremors recorded in recent years warrants closer scientific scrutiny to determine whether dormant geological structures beneath the region are becoming active again. title: A man received demands to repay a Rs 30,000 loan he never took, and faced legal proceedings that threatened his credit record; consumer commission order has now held two lenders responsible, directing them to clear his credit record and pay Rs 35,000 in compensation
text: AI generated image used for representative purpose NEW DELHI: A consumer commission in Chandigarh has held two lenders responsible for the harassment of a man who was pursued for a Rs 30,000 loan he says he never took. The loan was later found to be unauthorised. The commission directed CapFloat Financial Services, which operates under the brand name Axio, and Karur Vysya Bank to confirm he owes nothing, correct his credit record, and pay him Rs 25,000 as compensation and Rs 10,000 as litigation costs. In its order dated October 27, 2026, the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-I, Chandigarh, held that the conduct of the two companies amounted to âgross deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.â It dismissed the complaint against Amazon Pay India. How the dispute arose According to the order, the complainant, Daljeet Singh, a resident of Manimajra, received a text message in February 2024 demanding repayment of Rs 12,316 against a loan account. He said he had never applied for or availed of any such loan. When he enquired, CapFloat officials told him a credit facility of Rs 30,000 had been provided through Amazon Pay Later. He alleged that, despite his repeated requests and assurances, the company kept demanding repayment through recovery calls and threatening messages. He filed a police complaint on February 10, 2024. He later received summons from a Ludhiana court in recovery proceedings initiated by CapFloat for Rs 22,569. A legal notice dated April 20, 2025, then demanded Rs 32,694 as dues outstanding as of March 31, 2025. On April 27, 2025, he wrote to the company seeking documents on the loan application, sanction, disbursement and beneficiary account. In an email dated May 7, 2025, CapFloat said he had registered for Amazon Pay Later on January 14, 2024, and that 20 percent of the facility was funded by it and 80 percent by Karur Vysya Bank. It described the facility as a virtual line of credit, with no amount disbursed into any bank account. Singh alleged that the unauthorised loan and its adverse reporting in his CIBIL report hurt his creditworthiness and led another bank to refuse him a loan. The order does not record a finding on that last claim. What the companies said CapFloat told the commission that its investigation identified the matter as an account takeover case involving an unauthorised transaction on Amazonâs platform. After confirmation from Amazon, it said, it waived the entire facility on June 18, 2025, without admitting liability. It also said it informed the credit bureaus and the co-lender about clearing the historical overdue entries and closing the account, and that the changes were expected to show in his credit profile within 30 to 45 working days. The order does not verify whether the updates took place. CapFloat and Karur Vysya Bank further said Singh declined to provide copies of his Aadhaar and PAN for internal verification, citing legal advice, even though the registered mobile number was linked to him in the companyâs records. The commission did not rely on this point in its findings. Amazon Pay India said it could not trace any such loan using the mobile number provided and had no Amazon Pay Later account registered against it. It said it was only a facilitator and that CapFloat was responsible for clarifying the discrepancy. Karur Vysya Bank said the facility was offered under a co-lending arrangement with CapFloat, with the bank bearing 80 percent of the lending share and CapFloat 20 percent, and that CapFloat managed the accounting. It relied on CapFloatâs submission that the transaction had been found unauthorised and the loan waived. What the commission found The bench of president Pawanjit Singh and member Suresh Kumar Sardana noted that CapFloat, with Karur Vysya Bank relying on its submission, accepted that the transaction was an account takeover and that the complainant was not liable for the loan. The commission observed that these corrective steps came only after Singh had faced recovery demands and legal proceedings, and was at risk of damage to his creditworthiness. It noted that he had also approached the police and had to pursue the matter repeatedly to establish that he had not authorised the loan. âIt is also observed that through things have been corrected & set in order by the OPs No.1 & 2 [sic; the order appears to mean OP Nos. 1 and 3], but these steps were taken only after the complainant had faced recovery demands, legal proceedings and the risk of damage to his creditworthiness,â the commission said. It added that the subsequent waiver âdoes not absolveâ the opposite parties of responsibility for the âinconvenience, harassment and adverse consequencesâ suffered by the complainant due to the unauthorised transaction and its reporting to credit bureaus. Final order CapFloat and Karur Vysya Bank, jointly and severally, must: Issue a certificate confirming zero outstanding liability on the disputed loan account. Rectify incorrect and adverse entries relating to the account with the credit bureaus and co-lenders. Pay Rs 25,000 as compensation for mental agony and harassment. Pay Rs 10,000 as litigation costs. They must comply within 45 days of receiving a certified copy of the order. If the compensation is not paid within that period, the Rs 25,000 will carry simple interest at 9 percent per annum from the date of the order until it is paid. The complaint against Amazon Pay India was dismissed.

title: 'Seen it for a couple of years': New Zealand captain lauds Tilak Varma's growth as finisher after India's second T20I win
text: Tilak Varma New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner has seen Tilak Varma 's development at close quarters in the Mumbai Indians dressing room and believes the left-hander has grown into a reliable finisher, a role he underlined with an unbeaten 51 in India's four-wicket win in the second T20I. Santner, who returned figures of 4/21 in the match, recalled how Tilak initially batted at No. 3 for Mumbai Indians in the IPL before adapting to the demands of finishing games. Watch Mitchell Santner press conference: New Zealand captain on India's win, missed chances & more "When he (Tilak) first started, he was batting three. And it's a slightly different role. So I guess the middle order role depends on how you operate in the middle and in the death phase. I've seen it for a couple of years now at Mumbai. He's very good," Santner said after New Zealand's defeat. The New Zealand skipper also praised his IPL teammate Naman Dhir for his approach at the crease and acknowledged Nitish Kumar Reddy's contribution in the closing stages of India's chase. "And same with Naman Dhir. I think the way he's come in and just looks so free from the start. Tilak took his time a little bit today, but managed the chase very well with Reddy at the end. If you can finish off games as a finisher, you're doing a pretty good job. So, I think it was a great knock from those last three, especially tonight," he added. Despite his four-wicket haul, Santner felt New Zealand had let the match slip away through mistakes in the field. He pointed to dropped catches and missed opportunities in the latter stages of India's chase, saying the two sides had been closely matched in terms of their overall skills. "If you look at the skills of both teams, it's been very close and it's come down to some small moments in the field. I think especially us, the back end of that chase tonight. I think we're in a very good position, a couple of drop catches, missed fields. And it's the winning or losing of the game." Santner said New Zealand had played good cricket in both matches but needed to make better use of key moments. title: 'Why should I wake up at 5 am?': Sarfaraz Khan opens up on India snubs, motivation and father's support
text: Sarfaraz Khan (PTI Photo) MUMBAI: The shrug of the shoulder said it all when Sarfaraz Khan was asked about his absence from the India Test set-up. The latest snub came when he was overlooked for India A's three-match tour of New Zealand. This was after he had been included in the Test squad for the Sri Lanka tour as Sai Sudharsan's replacement. Quizzed about what keeps him motivated despite repeatedly being overlooked, the 29-year-old said he often finds himself questioning the effort he puts in every day. Watch Inside Gill and KL Rahul's intense training | Why no Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma | Nets footage "I wake up every morning and ask myself the same question. Why should I work harder? Why do the same things? Why should I wake up at 5 am (for practice)? I have already played for India. So even with basic effort, I can still play for Mumbai. With that effort, I can still get those 50s and 100s. So sometimes I start questioning it (the effort). But when I see Abbu (father Naushad) putting in that effort, I think of going out there and performing for him. So there is something or the other that keeps motivating me," said the Mumbai batter. Sarfaraz last played for India when New Zealand toured the country in 2024. He was also part of the squad for India's 2024-25 tour of Australia but did not get a game Down Under. He added: "Right now, the motivation is to play cricket. I don't like to sit at home. I think I'm made for cricket. Wherever I get an opportunity... Ranji Trophy , Mushtaq Ali, Vijay Hazare , IPL, or if the Indian team calls me. I just want to play cricket." As far as communication from the national selectors is concerned, Sarfaraz feels let down by the perception that he is only being considered for Indian conditions. "The selector didn't say it directly. But when I went with the Indian team, I heard that they are looking at me more for Indian conditions. But I will question that (thinking). I have scored centuries in South Africa and England (during intra-squad matches). In India, you get such big rank turners. You struggle so much when you come from domestic cricket. And suddenly, you will not be able to perform on such a difficult wicket. .. so you can't get more than 30-40 runs," said Sarfaraz, who made a 100-ball 55 on Day One of Mumbai's Group D match against Railways at the Brabourne Stadium on Monday. The centuries Sarfaraz is referring to came during intra-squad games. In 2023, he scored a 61-ball century in Pretoria, while during the 2025 England tour, he made a 76-ball 101 for India A against the Indian Test squad. Despite the setbacks, he focused on improving his fitness, and skills, in the off-season and shedding a few kilos as well. He has lost 22kg and now tips the scales at 77kg, having once weighed 97kg. Right now, he is looking forward to scoring runs in the domestic season and staying ready for an India call-up so that he is not found wanting. But when it comes to Sarfaraz, a tongue-in-cheek comment is never far away, even if his career is at a crossroads. "I used to play better when I was fat," he said cheekily, before adding: "It is not like I'm not getting runs. You can't get the same amount of runs every year. Sometimes it's up and down. As long as you are not out of form, you don't have to worry. In reality, my weight was more." Sarfaraz still boasts a healthy first-class record, having scored 5,354 runs in 66 matches at an average of 63.73, including 18 centuries. title: A Kerala passenger received â¹1 less on his cancelled train ticket and sued IRCTC; two years later, the consumer court ordered the railway corporation to pay â¹3,100 in compensation.
text: (Image Credit: Canva) A one-rupee shortfall in a train ticket refund led a passenger from Kerala to take the Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation ( IRCTC ) to the consumer commission. The passenger, who had booked and cancelled a ticket in 2024, won the case, with the Kasaragod District Consumer Commission directing IRCTC to pay â¹3,100 in compensation along with the pending refund amount. However, the refund rules applicable at the time have since been revised. The claimant cancelled his ticket on August 17, 2024, more than 48 hours before the scheduled journey on August 20, 2024. He booked an AC three-tier train ticket for â¹553 on August 11. The complaint mentions that IRCTC deducted â¹180 as cancellation charges and 5 per cent GST, which amounted to â¹9. As calculated, the refund amount came up to â¹341; however, IRCTC refunded only â¹340. This left a shortfall of â¹1. The shortfall caused the complainant confusion and mental distress. This incident caused a breach of trust towards India's primary railway organisation. His demands were â¹1 lakh for confusion, â¹1 lakh for breach of trust, â¹5,000 for litigation costs and the â¹1 shortfall. The commission rejected IRCTC's counter-argument because it was barred by limitation. It was noted that IRCTC did not attempt to justify the â¹1 shortage at the time of the refund. Failing to refund the exact amount was both a deficiency in service and an unfair trade practice. This created a liability for the organisation to refund the deficiency and pay additional compensation. The order by the commission mentioned, "Just because one rupee is paid less, the said fact really counts and the complainant is entitled to Rs 100 as compensation. Complainant is also eligible for the cost of litigation fixed as Rs 3,000." (Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons) The complainant's demands were partly granted. The â¹1 was compensated by paying Rs 100, and additionally, the consumer forum directed IRCTC to pay Rs 3,000 for litigation costs. "...complaint is allowed in part opposite party directed to refund Rs 1 with 9% interest from date of cancellation of date of ticket that is 17.08.2024 till realisation and Rs 100 towards compensation for deficiency in service and unfair trade practices and Rs 3000 as cost of litigation to the complainant within 30 days," the commission, chaired by Krishnan K, ordered. New Cancellation Policy of Indian Railways (Image Credit: Canva) Indian Railways has modified its cancellation and refund policy for confirmed tickets, with the revised rules coming into effect in March 2026. Under the new rules, all cancellation time windows have been increased, giving passengers less flexibility to cancel tickets at the last minute. Earlier, a full refund, after deducting the applicable flat cancellation charge, could be availed if the passenger cancelled tickets more than 48 hours before departure. Now, to get the highest possible refund, tickets must be cancelled more than 72 hours before departure. Thus, the amount refunded to the Kerala passenger would have differed had the new rules applied to his cancellation. Even the 25% and 50% deduction windows have also changed, moving from 48-12 hours to 72-24 hours and from 12-4 hours to 24-8 hours, respectively. Finally, the no-refund window has doubled from the earlier four hours to eight hours. Fully waitlisted e-tickets are automatically cancelled after chart preparation if all passengers remain waitlisted, subject to applicable clerkage deductions. One exception is confirmed Tatkal tickets, which generally receive no refund upon cancellation. However, passengers are eligible for a full refund if the Railways cancels the train. Thus, please plan your journeys ahead of time and avoid any last-minute changes to your plans. Indian Railways' revised policy means passengers may receive a lower refund for modifications made closer to their travel dates. title: 'The Big Show' is over: Glenn Maxwell announces retirement from international cricket
text: Glenn Maxwell (AFP Photo) Australian all-rounder Glenn Maxwell has announced his retirement from international cricket, bringing an end to a career in which he entertained fans with his aggressive batting and unusual shots. Maxwell made the announcement on Tuesday during an episode of The Final Word podcast. His decision also includes his retirement from domestic 50-over and four-day cricket for Victoria. Maxwell, popularly known as 'The Big Show', represented Australia in 149 ODIs, 130 T20Is and seven Test matches. He was part of Australia's 2015 and 2023 ODI World Cup-winning teams and also played a key role in the team's T20 World Cup triumph in 2021. Watch Gautam Gambhir on India's challenges, young players & ODI series "I'm going to be announcing my retirement from international cricket and domestic games for Victoria in the 50 over and the four-day stuff, red ball completely," the 38-year-old told The Final Word podcast in an episode released on Tuesday. Wants to focus on fitness Maxwell said he wants to give more attention to his fitness and prepare his body for the remaining tournaments in his career. "It's probably a time where I probably need to spend a little bit more time investing in the body to make sure I can get through the remaining couple of tournaments I've got in my career." He scored 3,990 runs in ODIs and 2,897 runs in T20 internationals. His last appearance for Australia came against Oman at the T20 World Cup in Sri Lanka in February. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Maxwell also made a special mark in T20 cricket. Along with India's Rohit Sharma, he remains one of only two players to score five international centuries in the format. With his off-spin bowling, he also picked up 128 wickets for Australia in the two shorter formats. Misses chance for MCG farewell Maxwell had retired from ODI cricket last year but was hoping to play one final international match at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG). However, that possibility ended when Australia announced its squad for the upcoming series against England on Monday. The selectors have focused on younger players in their short-format plans. Maxwell admitted that he had hoped to get a farewell match at his home ground but understood the team's decision. "There was, I suppose, a small hope or discussion that I might have been able to potentially get a send-off game at the MCG, but I can completely understand the direction they're going with this squad," he said. title: 'Chapter is maybe closed': R Ashwin fears Bhuvneshwar Kumar's India career could be over
text: Bhuvneshwar Kumar (BCCI Photo) Ravichandran Ashwin feels Bhuvneshwar Kumar could find it difficult to return to the Indian team after his disappointing comeback in the T20I series against New Zealand. The former India spinner believes the door may have closed for the experienced pacer and has backed Mohammed Shami to get another opportunity. Bhuvneshwar returned to India's T20I side after a gap of four years but failed to make a strong impression. The 36-year-old managed just one wicket in four matches and conceded 180 runs. Watch Gautam Gambhir on India's challenges, young players & ODI series Speaking on his YouTube channel, Ashwin said Bhuvneshwar's performances in the series were nowhere close to the form he showed in IPL 2026. "Bhuvneshwar Kumar hasn't bowled that well; he didn't prove his form," Ashwin said. "There was a night and day difference between his IPL form and here (New Zealand series). I think that chapter is maybe closed. It's very difficult. How will he come back?" he added. Bhuvneshwar fails to make an impact Bhuvneshwar earned his India comeback after an impressive IPL 2026 season, where he picked up 28 wickets in 16 matches and was arguably the best bowler of the tournament. However, he struggled to carry that form into the New Zealand series. In the opening T20I, he went wicketless and conceded 49 runs in four overs at an economy rate of 12.25. He picked up his only wicket of the series in the second match, dismissing Daryl Mitchell for six. However, he gave away 50 runs in his four overs. The experienced pacer failed to take a wicket in the third T20I as well, conceding 40 runs. He missed the fourth match before returning for the series finale, where he again went wicketless and conceded 41 runs. Overall, he finished the series with one wicket and an economy rate of 11.50. Ashwin questions Bhuvneshwar's preparation Ashwin felt the difference in Bhuvneshwar's bowling intensity and speed was a major concern. He also questioned whether the pacer had prepared well enough before the series. "Leave performance, leave giving extra runs. It's not that. What was disappointing, I felt the way he bowls in the IPL - the intensity, his run-up speed was lower, and his bowling speed was also lower. That tells me maybe he didn't come in prime training form for this series," Ashwin pointed out. He also explained why selectors could find it difficult to give an experienced player another opportunity after such a performance. "If that's the condition, the selectors will also think, 'Is this the way'? If you're a new kid or a young boy, you'll get ten chances. But you're an experienced guy coming back," he further said. text: How Sabrina Ionescu turned rejection into an NCAA record and WNBA championship(Getty Images) Ionescuâs success is about a lot more than what she has accomplished for the New York Liberty. The No. 1 overall pick in the 2020 WNBA Draft, she has evolved into one of the leagueâs best guards, helping lead New York to its first WNBA title in 2024, and she captured an Olympic gold medal with Team USA at Paris 2024 to cement her place in the sport. What drives Sabrina Ionescuâs endorsement and brand success Nike stays at the heart of Ionescuâs reputation. She was the first womenâs basketball player to have a unisex signature footwear and apparel collection with the company in 2023. The Sabrina line has continued to grow; Nike announced the Sabrina 4 collection in April 2026 and launched it in July. Her presence in both womenâs and menâs basketball has helped make her a recognizable name in performance footwear. Her broader endorsement portfolio has included partnerships with AT&T, BodyArmor, Fanatics, State Farm, Xbox and others. These partnerships allow her basketball audience to engage with companies and Ionescu to create a public profile outside of her performances on the court; in 2025, Forbes estimated her total earnings at $10.5 million, a sign of the growing weight of commercial opportunities in her overall financial picture. How Sabrina Ionescu balances basketball and business interests Ionescu has also studied investments in sports and technology. She became an investor and commercial advisor to Bay FC, a National Womenâs Soccer League club based in the San Francisco Bay Area, in March 2025. She is involved in contributing to commercial strategy and helping the clubâs athletes develop their own endorsement portfolios. The move is more of an interest in helping the growth of womenâs sports in general than just basketball. Her investments have also included Buzzer Media and Nex, and her work with Kevin Durantâs Boardroom and Thirty Five Ventures has broadened her exposure to sports media and business. title: Rohit Sharma's 5th T20I century and two super overs: A look at what happened when India last played in Bengaluru as IND vs WI set for series decider at Chinnaswamy
text: Rohit Sharma plays a shot during the third T20 cricket match between India and Afghanistan, at M Chinnaswamy Stadium, in Bengaluru. (PTI Photo) Shai Hope struck another century as West Indies beat India by 24 runs in the fourth Twenty20 in Hyderabad on Wednesday to level the five-match series at 2-2. Chasing 248, India got off to a quick start, with Sanju Samson reaching his half-century in just 20 balls before Keemo Paul dismissed him for 56. Watch Shafali Verma on vice-captaincy, India's fearless cricket & World Cup glory Shreyas Iyer added 16 off 11 balls, while Abhishek Sharma scored 29 before Gudakesh Motie sent the opener back. India mounted another push towards the end through Nitish Kumar Reddy and Tilak Varma, who put together 70 runs off just 32 balls to keep the chase alive. Varma was dismissed for 43, while Paul removed Reddy and took two more wickets in the 19th over, bringing India's chase to a halt. The lower order could not offer much resistance as India were bowled out for 223. Bengaluru will host the series-deciding T20I on Saturday. What happened when India last played a T20I in Bengaluru India last played a T20I in Bengaluru on January 17, 2024, when they faced Afghanistan in the third and final match of the series. India had already secured the series by winning the first two games. But the final match was far from a dead rubber. It produced a series of dramatic moments, including two Super Overs and a controversial episode involving Rohit Sharma. In the first Super Over, Afghanistan's Mohammad Nabi and Rahmanullah Gurbaz ran extra runs after the ball deflected off Nabi's body on the final delivery. The incident left Virat Kohli angry, with the India batter seen clapping in Nabi's face. The drama continued moments later. With two runs needed off the final ball of first super over, Rohit, who was at the non-striker's end, walked off to allow Rinku Singh to take over the running. However, Yashasvi Jaiswal's bottom edge went straight to the wicketkeeper, and India could manage only a single, leaving the first Super Over tied. Rohit was ready to bat again in the second Super Over. Under point 22 of Appendix F of the playing conditions, a batter who had retired could return only if the retirement had been due to injury, illness or "any other unavoidable cause". Earlier in the match, Rohit had won the toss and elected to bat. India suffered a disastrous start, losing four wickets inside the powerplay. Jaiswal fell at 18 in the third over, Kohli was dismissed at the same score in the fourth, Shivam Dube departed at 21, and India lost their fourth wicket at 22. Rohit kept the innings together and combined with Rinku for a 190-run partnership for the fifth wicket. India recovered from 22/4 to finish at 212/4, with Rohit scoring 121 off 69 balls and Rinku making 69 off 38 deliveries. Rohit became the first batter to score five centuries in T20 internationals, rescuing India from a position where they had lost four wickets for just 22 runs. Afghanistan matched India's total, forcing the match into a Super Over. Gulbadin Naib led their fightback with 55 off 23 balls. Naib and Gurbaz came out to bat in the first Super Over, which was bowled by Mukesh Kumar. A mix-up between the batters resulted in Naib being run out. Gurbaz and Nabi then scored runs before the controversial final delivery. The batters ran a bye, but the throw from wicketkeeper Sanju Samson deflected off Nabi's leg towards long-on. The pair ran two more runs. Rohit and his teammates were unhappy with the outcome, though the running was within the rules. India needed 17 runs to win the first Super Over. Rohit hit Azmatullah Omarzai for two successive sixes to leave India needing three runs off the final two balls. With two runs required from the last delivery, Rohit retired hurt to allow Rinku, the quicker runner, to take over. But Jaiswal could only edge the ball towards the wicketkeeper, and India managed just one run, leaving the Super Over tied. title: UK Labour minister under fire for claiming employers are not âworking peopleâ
text: File photo: Britain's Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds A British treasury minister has reignited a political row over Labourâs definition of âworking peopleâ after saying employers do not fall under the category, drawing criticism from opposition politicians who accused the government of overlooking the contribution of small-business owners. Chief secretary to the treasury Emma Reynolds made the remarks during an interview with GB News on Sunday. Asked about people affected by Labourâs economic policies, Reynolds said: âI donât think employers are working people, they are companies.â When host Camilla Tominey asked whether that meant she was not a working person because she employed a cleaner, Reynolds replied: âNo, but youâre an employee probably of your company, and Iâm saying there is a difference between employers and employees.â The comments prompted a backlash from Conservative politicians. Shadow business minister Bradley Thomas accused Labour of displaying a âpatronising, out-of-touchâ attitude towards small businesses, pointing to electricians who take on apprentices and shop owners who employ young people for weekend work. Shadow work and pensions minister Helen Whately said the remarks showed that Labour did not understand that businesses were built through hard work. Shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge also criticised the distinction, saying employing people was among the hardest parts of running a business. The exchange has revived scrutiny of Labourâs 2024 manifesto pledge not to raise taxes on âworking peopleâ, including income tax, national insurance and VAT. The pledge became contentious after former chancellor Rachel Reeves raised employersâ national insurance contributions in October 2024. The government argued that the increase did not breach the commitment because it applied to employers rather than employees. The main rate of employersâ national insurance rose from 13.5% to 15%, while the secondary threshold â the level above which employers begin paying the contribution â was reduced from Â£9,100 to Â£5,000. A Treasury spokesperson defended the governmentâs position, saying it would stick to its manifesto commitments and would not increase the rates of income tax, employee national insurance, VAT or corporation tax. title: Police arrest drug case accused on the run for two years from Kullu

The limit is 100 kmph on four-lane roads and 70 kmph on other roads. The prescribed limits for other categories of vehicles are lower. The rules provide a limited relaxation for vehicles travelling up to 5% above the notified speed limit, beyond which the exemption from challans does not apply. This means the existing provision does not support a relaxation of 20% for cars on expressways. title: Dhinidhi Desinghu scripts history with first-ever Indian swimming medal at Youth Olympics
text: Dhinidhi Desinghu (File photo) BENGALURU: Indian swimming has a new milestone to celebrate, and Bengaluru talent Dhinidhi Desinghu is at the heart of it. The 16-year-old became the first swimmer from the country to win a medal at the Youth Olympic Games, claiming bronze in the women's 100m freestyle in Dakar, Senegal, on Monday. While Dhinidhi had set her sights on gold and a sub-55-second finish, her podium finish was a historic achievement for Indian swimming. Croatia's Ana Bobanovic took gold in 55.89 seconds, while New Zealand's Alyssa Lawson claimed silver in 56.13 seconds. The performance had been building momentum from the heats. Dhinidhi clocked 56.80 seconds to finish third-fastest overall and become the first Indian female swimmer to qualify for a Youth Olympics final. She carried that form into the final. âI'm very happy but also at a loss for words. In the heats, my timing went below 57. I've never had a time below 57 in the event, and I knew something special would happen," she told TOI. Going into the final, there was a mix of nerves and confidence. The conditions, too, worked in her favour. "Generally, when I swim outdoors, and it's hot and humid, I swim better, because the conditions are similar to what it is back home," she said. The result, however, was initially not quite what she had hoped for. "When I touched the pad and saw the timing, I wasn't very happy. I wanted to win gold and I wanted my time to break 55, but didnât achieve either. But slowly it sank in â I am India's first swimmer to win a medal at the Youth Olympics and that does mean something special," added the teenager, who trains under Nihar Ameen. The win's significance went beyond the medal itself. Dhinidi believes her podium finish is a breakthrough for women's swimming in the country. "I think what makes it more special is that it's a woman who has given India its first medal in swimming in the competition. It will mean a lot for women's swimming because we're not at the same level as the men. This will make it a memorable chapter in women's swimming in our country and help in the growth of our sport," she said. But milestones are nothing new to her. Dhinidhi was just 14 when she made her Olympic debut at Paris 2024, becoming the youngest member of the Indian contingent. She had also represented India at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou and the 2024 World Aquatics Championships in Doha. For now, the triumph is still sinking in. âIt (medal) will take some time to sink in. After Paris, it took a couple of years to sink in that I was an Olympian. We would want to win because of something we've not done forever in India, so it would have been nice. I think the cup still is in our favour because we won the home leg the last time we played (in 2023) 3-2,â Sammy told reporters in the post-match press conference. He added that the team's ability to match India and outperform them in certain areas showed how much progress the players had made. âWe understand what success means to us; we don't ever take for granted where we are as a team and the challenges that we face. We just look to make those strides, and I think after this series we've taken a massive step. We played against the defending champions, and we've matched them (and) in certain areas we've outplayed them, especially in their backyard,â he added. Sammy calls for financial support Beyond the team's results, Sammy stressed that West Indies cricket needs financial backing to secure its future. title: WMO reports record-high Greenhouse Gas levels in 2025, says the long lifetime of CO2 commits planet to warmer future
text: NEW DELHI: Levels of globally averaged surface concentrations of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases (GHGs) - methane and nitrous oxide - in the atmosphere reached âunprecedented highsâ in 2025, locking in more long-term temperature increase for the planet, said a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Tuesday. It noted that the intensifying El Nino may lead to a further surge as this climatic phenomenon of warming of ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Equatorial Pacific has the potential to reduce the efficiency of the biosphere to absorb carbon dioxide. The report is one of the WMOâs flagship annual publications in which it shared levels of GHG concentrations - the amount of gas that accumulates in the atmosphere - and not new annual emissions. Since about half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere and it has a very long lifetime, it leads to a rise in its levels of concentration that traps heat and eventually contributes to a warmer future. âThe past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. CO2 has a very long lifetime and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries,â said WMO deputy secretary-general Ko Barrett. The report noted that though the increase in CO2 from 2024 to 2025 was lower than the anomalously high increase from 2023 to 2024, it was slightly higher than the average annual growth rate over the last decade (2016â2025). âThe more modest growth rate from 2024 to 2025 reflects recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino, which reduced the efficiency of the biosphere through more drought, drier vegetation and more wildfires,â said WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova. The annual GHG Index, flagged by the report, shows that from 1990 to 2025, radiative forcing â the warming effect on climate â by long-lived greenhouse gases increased by 56%, with CO2 accounting for about 81% of this increase and its growth rates having tripled since the 1960s. Quantitatively, the globally averaged surface concentration of CO2 in 2025 was 426.8 parts per million, or 153% of the 1750 pre-industrial baseline. Concentrations of methane and nitrous oxide â the second and third most important long-lived greenhouse gases related to human activities â also rose to new records. Methane accounts for about 16% of the warming effect on climate by long-lived GHG but it has a much shorter lifetime than CO2. Approximately 35% of methane is emitted into the atmosphere by natural sources (for example, wetlands) which are sensitive to climate as well, and about 65% comes from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, fossil fuel exploitation, landfills and biomass burning. âThe globally averaged methane concentration in 2025 was 1948 parts per billion (ppb) â or 267% of the 1750 level,â said the WMO in its annual bulletin, which provides authoritative scientific information for negotiators at the UN Climate conference.
